at.step: Algorithm R: keep the first k items. For every item after that, draw a number uniformly from one through how many items have been seen, and if it lands at k or below, replace that slot.

By induction: if every item was uniformly in the reservoir after n items, then after the next item each survivor’s probability multiplies by one minus a shrinking fraction, and the product telescopes to exactly k over n plus one.

Algorithm L draws the skip length itself from a geometric distribution, then jumps straight to the next item that enters the reservoir — three random numbers for every item that enters, nothing spent on the rest.

At the same million-item scale, a seeded run of Algorithm L makes a few thousand draws against Algorithm R’s hundreds of thousands — on the order of k times one plus the log of n over k, not n minus k.
Each item draws a key: a uniform random number raised to the power of one over its own weight. The sample is the k items whose keys are largest, held in a min-heap of size k.

Four items of equal weight and one item ten times as heavy, sampling two: the heavy item is kept nearly every time, not by the naive share of the total weight doubled — that guess is not even a valid probability.

Two uniform reservoirs merge into one by sending each output slot to the larger stream’s reservoir more often, in proportion to how many items that stream actually saw — so a reservoir without its own count cannot be merged. A real range partitioner carries exactly that count with every sample it takes.

items.item: what the skip actually saves differs between a sequential stream and a seekable source

at.step: The skip saves random draws either way, but on a stream read item by item it saves only that — the reading itself still happens one item at a time. Only an indexed, seekable source lets the skip save the reads too.
